card pr-gate  [decided]
A written rule is enforced by a check when a record moves to a new state
why: A rule that exists only as prose is not enforced. Over time the records stop following their own rules.
subtree: 7 cards, 7 decided

A pipeline has rules about its records. Example: a ticket may only move to Done if it has a linked pull request. If this rule is only prose in a skill file, an agent can forget it. Nobody notices, and the records drift.

The rule becomes a small program, a check. The check runs at the moment a record changes state. In the example, it runs when the ticket moves to Done. It does not run when the ticket is created, because a new ticket has no pull request yet.

**Example.** An agent runs `tracker status T-12 done`.
1. The check looks for a linked pull request on T-12.
2. It finds none, so the move fails.
3. The check prints the next command: `tracker link T-12 <pr-url>`.
4. The agent runs that command, then repeats the move. It passes.

AgentRuntime is Claude Code headless today, and the Claude Agent SDK later, with Codex as a further, harder test of vendor-independence (see #pr-iface:opt1). Bus is a JSONL file today, a real event store later — the append-only log that is the spine (#pr-log): every state change is one event, and it is the only thing Renderer and Tracker's outward publish ever read.

Four names, four jobs:
- Tracker: the external issue tracker (Linear, GitHub Issues). Seven verbs only — getBrief, setBrief, addNote, setStage, listByStage, linkPR, linkDependsOn (#tk-verbs). It is a one-way publish target; a change made directly in the tracker never writes back to the log (#tracker).
- AgentRuntime: whatever executes a work item. Given a task, it runs the agent and returns its events.
- Bus: the append-only event log. Every state change the loop controller makes becomes one event here, and nowhere else.
- Renderer: turns the Bus into something a human can see. The werk map today, something else later.

## The boundary

A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.

A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.

The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

## A prompt holds no control flow

A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. The sentence "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop. A loop is code, so it goes in the program, not in the prompt.

## Why

An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time. A product needs the rule followed every time (#pr-gate). A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness, so a pipeline made of skills cannot become a standalone product (#product).

## Scope

This card says where the logic lives. It does not say when the standalone engine is built. That timing is #pr-now. The engine's adapters are #pr-iface.

I staged a new body for #pr-logic as a proposal. It is on the card now as a diff. It adds four sections:
1. **The boundary.** A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result, for example a state change, a contract check, a retry cap, or a merge. A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement, for example a spec, a grade, or a review. The prompt returns an answer, and the program decides what happens next.
2. **A prompt holds no control flow.** "If the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop, so it goes in code.
3. **Why.** It links to #pr-gate (a rule in prose is followed only most of the time) and to #product (a prompt runs inside one harness only).
4. **Scope.** This card says where the logic lives. The question of *when* to build the engine goes to #pr-now and #pr-iface.

The scope section has one effect: the postpone reason ("do not build the standalone engine yet") no longer applies to this card. It applies to #pr-now, which is already paused. #pr-logic can then become `decided`, and #werk-contract stops depending on an open card.

## What #pr-logic decides

A pipeline has steps and rules. For example: "run the checks", "if they fail, try again up to 5 times", and "a card cannot become decided without a reason". These rules can live in one of two places:

| | **A: skill files** (#pr-logic:opt0) | **B: a program** (#pr-logic) |
|---|---|---|
| Where the rule lives | Markdown text that the agent reads | Code in a CLI |
| Who runs the loop | The agent reads "retry 5 times" and does it | The program counts to 5 |
| What the agent does | Everything | Only the steps that need judgement: write code, grade, review |
| If the agent forgets a rule | Nothing stops it | The program refuses the action |
| Cost of a change | Edit a sentence | Edit code and tests |
| Runs outside Claude Code | No | Yes |

The card chooses B.

## You saw it work in the last turn

I ran `werk status pr-logic decided`. The CLI refused, because the card had no `depends_on` link and no kill criterion. That refusal is #pr-logic in action. With option A, `AGENTS.md` would say "always add depends_on", and an agent could skip it. That happened two times before: #ro-unchal and #vi-backend.

`werk build` is the same case. The code runs the checks, caps the retries, and enforces the 60-second limit. `claude -p` only writes code, and the grader only grades.

## What it does not decide

- **When to build the standalone engine.** #pr-now decides that, and #pr-now is paused.
- **Which adapters the engine has** (Tracker, AgentRuntime, and the others). #pr-iface decides that.

The card was `open` only because of the "not now" timing. The new Scope section moves that timing to #pr-now.

Eryk, 2026-09-20, on #werk-loop: "cards must be worded only about themselves not the outer
world, not about the planning process."

The card's why had read "Planning is scoped enough to build werk from scratch. The next thing
to prove is that the plan can be executed by the loop." His objection: that the planning loop
is scoped enough does not help anyone decide anything about the build loop.

**Why:** a card is read later, cold, by a person or an agent that needs to act on its subject.
State-of-the-session facts are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight. Titles too —
"werk v0 ships the inner build loop" became "Inner build loop"; the scope claim belonged in a
`refines` edge to #werk, not in the words.

**How to apply:** cut "Eryk, <date>:" openers, "from him", "Scope cut", "the next thing to
prove", and comparisons to where the planning conversation stands. Keep the decision, the
reasoning, and the measurements. Put the scope claim in an edge. Attribution lives in `who`
and in the log, not in prose. Records of a reversal are still fair game — a superseded card
should say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but that is about the
subject, not about the session. See [[feedback_record_options_live]].

Confirmed again 2026-09-22 on #st-gates: a sentence read "G3 is new: #stages previously said
gates stop at the PR — that no longer holds." Same defect as above, one level down — "is new"
and "previously said" narrate the card's own edit history instead of stating the current fact.
Fixed to "G3 sits after production measurement, at the end of validate, closing the loop back
to intent." Watch for this exact shape: "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "no longer holds/
applies" — describing what the card said before is still narrating the session, even when the
subject being discussed is the card itself rather than the outer world. State the current fact
plainly; if the change in reading matters, put it in the log/edges, not the prose.

The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller go into a small TypeScript CLI. A skill file becomes a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.

## The boundary

A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.

A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.

The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

## A prompt holds no control flow

A prompt is text that the program builds and sends. T
